statement-scope.text: Choose an eye point EEE and a canvas plane Π\PiΠ. To paint an object so that it looks undistorted from EEE, imagine it drawn normally on a picture plane Π′\Pi'Π′ perpendicular to the central line of sight from EEE and through its intersection with Π\PiΠ, and then project it from EEE onto Π\PiΠ: each point PPP of the intended picture is painted where the line EPEPEP crosses the canvas.Require every intended ray from EEE to have a finite forward intersection with the canvas. For those rays, the painted canvas and intended picture send the eye the same directions, so they look identical from EEE. A ray parallel to the canvas has no finite intersection, and an intersection behind the eye cannot supply that intended view. Seen from anywhere else, the painting is a smear: if the line of sight meets the canvas at the angle φ\varphiφ, the central local scale along the tilt is 1/sin⁡φ1/\sin\varphi1/sinφ, which is large for a grazing point of view. This is a differential scale at that central intersection; a finite image undergoes a projective warp with position-dependent scale.Exact for a flat canvas, a single fixed eye, and intended rays with finite forward canvas intersections. Extreme offered grazing settings can violate that ray condition and lose part of the intended picture; the projection is exact only on the remaining valid rays. The stated central local scale does not assert a complete finite picture at those settings. Two eyes and a viewer who knows the trick soften the illusion in practice.

proof.text: This is central projection (art-1.2) used backwards. A perspective picture is the cross-section of the visual pyramid with the canvas; the intended picture and its shadow on the canvas are two cross-sections of the same pyramid, so from the apex they cover each other exactly. At the central intersection of the two picture planes, the derivative of this projection has scale 1/sin⁡φ1/\sin\varphi1/sinφ along the tilt and scale one in the perpendicular direction. Away from that point its scale changes with position; the finite projection is not a uniform stretch. This explains the long anamorphic image without replacing the computed projective map by an affine one.

caption.text: The gold eye is the painter's point, set by the angle and distance sliders; the blue handle in the plan is the viewer. When every intended ray has a finite forward canvas intersection, putting the viewer on the gold point gives the undistorted intended skull on the right. Very grazing settings may lose part of the picture through parallel rays or intersections behind the eye; the canvas label is only the central local scale. Drag the viewer away, or press “in front”, and the skull collapses into the smear again.
